meaning: Lists things that happen one after another: “what with A and B, (it was awful)”. Usually has a complaining, exasperated tone.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + わ, verb / i-adjective plain form + わで

senses.label: When it rains, it pours
senses.meaning: Lists several bad things that happen at once or in a row. The second half is usually an overall judgment like 「大変だ」 or 「散々だ」. The tone is “what bad luck, I've had enough”.
senses.connection: A plain form + わ, B plain form + わで, ... (common: 降るわ, 吹くわ, なくすわ, 遅れるわ)
examples: What with the rain and the wind, the trip was a disaster.
I lost my wallet and missed my train. What a terrible day.
My kid has a fever and work is busy, so I don't even have time to rest.

senses.label: Over the top
senses.meaning: The same or similar verbs are repeated to show an action going on and on to an amazing degree. It isn't always bad; it often describes a lively or chaotic scene.
senses.connection: Dictionary form + わ + dictionary form + わで (食べるわ飲むわで, 泣くわわめくわで)
examples: At the year-end party, everyone ate and drank and made a huge racket.
The lost child cried and screamed, and nobody could calm him down.

notes: This is quite colloquial and is generally not used in formal writing.
「わ」 follows the plain form, never 「です・ます」. Nouns and na-adjectives take 「〜だわ」, but this is rare.
The second half is often an evaluation of the whole situation, like 「大変だった」, 「散々だった」, or 「さんざんな目にあった」.

daily.title: Complaining to a friend
daily.description: Back from a trip, you complain to a friend about all your bad luck.
daily.example: The flight was late and my luggage got lost. I'm exhausted.

daily.title: Describing a party
daily.description: Telling your family how lively yesterday's party was.
daily.example: Yesterday everyone sang and danced. It was a blast.

daily.title: After moving house
daily.description: Chatting with a neighbor about the chaos on moving day.
daily.example: On moving day it rained and the truck didn't show up. It was rough.

work.title: Chatting about overtime
work.description: At the end of the month, you chat with a coworker about recent trouble at work. Casual office talk.
work.example: This month problems kept popping up and deadlines piled up, so I didn't get any rest.

etymology: The 「わ」 is thought to come from the sentence-final particle 「わ」, which adds emotion or emphasis. Repeating 「〜わ〜わ」 “sighs out” each event one by one, and the 「で」 of cause or state is added, giving “what with A and B, (the result was ...)”.

similar.title: 〜わ〜わ
similar.explanation: 「〜わ〜わ」 can simply list things or end a sentence as an exclamation. 「〜わ〜わで」 adds 「で」, so it must be followed by a summary, as in 「〜わ〜わで大変だった」.

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: 「〜やら〜やら」 also lists several things, but it is more neutral and can describe happy feelings too (嬉しいやら恥ずかしいやら). 「〜わ〜わで」 is more colloquial and mostly used for complaining.

similar.title: 〜たり〜たりする
similar.explanation: 「〜たり〜たり」 just gives examples objectively. 「〜わ〜わで」 stresses that things happen one after another, with complaint or amazement.

similar.title: 〜し
similar.explanation: 「〜し〜し」 lists reasons in a calm tone. 「〜わ〜わで」 carries the strong feeling that things are a total mess.

meaning: A strengthened negative: “not at all, definitely won't”. It shows the speaker's firm conviction, annoyance, or scorn.
connection: Verb masu-stem + やしない (casual) / はしない; verb te-form + やしない

senses.label: Definitely won't
senses.meaning: The speaker firmly states that something won't happen. Much stronger than 「〜ない」. Often used for resolve, to argue back, or to reassure someone.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + はしない / やしない (負けやしない, 忘れはしない, 逃げはしない)
examples: I will never forget you as long as I live.
I'm not going to lose over something like this.
Don't worry, nobody's going to get angry.

senses.label: Not ... at all
senses.meaning: Shows annoyance or contempt about the situation: “doesn't ... at all, never even ...”. 「やしない」 is the usual form here, and it is very colloquial.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + やしない (わかりやしない, できやしない); verb te-form + やしない (聞いてやしない)
examples: Nobody could understand an explanation this difficult.
No matter how many times I tell that kid, he just doesn't listen.
He couldn't possibly do it alone, yet he turned down help.

notes: 「やしない」 is a casual sound change of 「はしない」. It is more informal and often sounds annoyed. In formal situations use 「〜はしない」 or just 「〜ない」.
The polite forms are 「〜やしません」 and 「〜はしません」. The past is 「〜やしなかった」.
In 「においはしない」 or 「音はしない」, 「は」 marks the topic and 「しない」 means “there is no (smell / sound)”. This is not this grammar point.

daily.title: Reassuring a friend
daily.description: Your friend is worried about being blamed, and you say it'll be fine.
daily.example: It's fine. Nobody's going to hate you over something like that.

daily.title: Complaining about family
daily.description: A mother complains that her child never listens.
daily.example: No matter how often I tell him, he never tidies up.

daily.title: Showing determination
daily.description: Words to yourself or your teammates before a match.
daily.example: I won't give up until the very end.

work.title: Reading a novel
work.description: A character in a novel makes a vow. In writing it is often 「〜はしない」.
work.example: I will never forget the humiliation of that day.

work.title: Grumbling with a coworker
work.description: A coworker privately complains that the boss never reads reports. Only between people who are close.
work.example: The department head never reads the reports anyway.

etymology: Formed from verb masu-stem + the topic particle 「は」 + 「しない」. 「は」 singles out the action and negates it, which strengthens the negation. In speech, 「は (wa)」 merges with the vowel before it and becomes 「や」, giving 「〜やしない」.

similar.title: 〜っこない
similar.explanation: 「〜っこない」 means “there's no way ...”, focusing on zero possibility (できっこない). 「〜やしない」 can also show annoyance that someone simply doesn't do something.

similar.title: 〜ものか
similar.explanation: 「〜ものか」 uses a rhetorical question to show firm denial and resolve (負けるものか). 「〜やしない」 is a direct negation, slightly calmer.

similar.title: 〜もしない (not even)
similar.explanation: 「〜もしない」 stresses “doesn't even do this much”. 「〜はしない／やしない」 only strengthens the negation and has no “not even” meaning.

meaning: Lists one thing or demand after another: “now it's A, now it's B”. Usually sounds fed up or annoyed.
connection: やれ + noun (だ), やれ + noun (だ) と / だの

senses.label: One thing after another
senses.meaning: Lists events or activities that keep coming: “first it's A, then it's B”. It suggests there's too much to handle and sounds weary.
senses.connection: やれ + noun + だ, やれ + noun + だと (やれ会議だ、やれ出張だと)
examples: What with meetings one day and business trips the next, my father always looks busy.
At the end of the year, what with year-end parties and the big cleanup, I never get to relax.

senses.label: Nagging demands
senses.meaning: Lists someone's various demands, complaints, or excuses: “first they want A, then B”. Often used with 「だの」 or 「と」 and shows the speaker's annoyance.
senses.connection: やれ + noun / plain form + だの, やれ + noun / plain form + だのと (言う, うるさい)
examples: My mom keeps nagging me: “Study!”, “Go to bed early!”
She's always complaining: she's cold, she's hungry.
The customer started complaining that the food was slow and the taste was bland.

notes: 「やれ」 usually appears at least twice. A single 「やれ」 doesn't make this pattern.
The interjection 「やれやれ」 (“phew”, “oh well”) shows relief or resignation and is different.
The 「やれ」 in 「宿題をやれ」 is the command form of 「やる」 and isn't this pattern either.

daily.title: Complaining about parents
daily.description: A teenager complains to a friend that their parents are too strict.
daily.example: My parents are so annoying: curfew this, grades that.

daily.title: Talking about a child's demands
daily.description: Parents chat about kids always wanting things.
daily.example: My kid keeps asking for a video game, then for comics. It's exhausting.

work.title: Reading an essay
work.description: An essay or column describing how busy modern people are.
work.example: What with work and social obligations, people today have no time for themselves.

work.title: Chatting with a coworker
work.description: A coworker complains about a client's many change requests.
work.example: That client is so demanding: change the design, move up the deadline.

etymology: 「やれ」 was originally a call or exclamation (like 「やあ」 or 「それ」). It is thought to have come to introduce each item in a list. Repeating 「やれ〜やれ〜」 sounds like ticking off complaints one by one, which gives it a fed-up tone.

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: 「〜やら〜やら」 comes after each item and can show mixed feelings (嬉しいやら悲しいやら). 「やれ〜やれ〜」 comes before each item and is mostly used for weary complaining.

similar.title: 〜わ〜わで
similar.explanation: 「〜わ〜わで」 lists bad things that happen in a row. 「やれ〜やれ〜」 usually lists other people's demands or endless tasks.

similar.title: 〜たり〜たりする
similar.explanation: 「〜たり〜たり」 gives examples neutrally. 「やれ〜やれ〜」 clearly shows dissatisfaction and weariness.

title: 〜ぞ・〜ぜ (sentence-final particles)
meaning: Sentence-final particles that add emphasis. 「ぞ」 is used to psych yourself up or to warn someone; 「ぜ」 is used to assert something or invite someone forcefully.
connection: Plain form + ぞ / ぜ (nouns and na-adjectives can attach directly or as 「だぞ／だぜ」)

senses.label: Psyching yourself up
senses.meaning: Said to yourself to get motivated or make up your mind, like “All right, let's do this!”. Often with 「よし」 or 「さあ」.
senses.connection: Dictionary form / volitional form + ぞ (行くぞ, 頑張るぞ, やるぞ)
examples: All right, today I'm really going to give it my all!
OK, let's go.

senses.label: Reminding / warning
senses.meaning: Emphasizes something to the listener as a reminder or warning: “I'm telling you ...”. Forceful and mainly masculine; not used to superiors or elders.
senses.connection: Plain form + ぞ (危ないぞ, 遅れるぞ, 知らないぞ)
examples: Hurry up or you'll be late.
Hey, it's dangerous over there.
If you lie to me, I won't forgive you.

senses.label: Friendly assertion
senses.meaning: 「ぜ」 is used with close friends to state an opinion or make an invitation forcefully. It sounds breezy and a bit rough. It feels more directed at the listener than 「ぞ」.
senses.connection: Plain form + ぜ; volitional form + ぜ (行こうぜ, やろうぜ)
examples: Come on, let's get started.
This ramen is awesome.

notes: Both 「ぞ」 and 「ぜ」 are very casual and strongly masculine. Don't use them with superiors, customers, or in formal settings.
「ぜ」 is even more casual and a bit tough-guy. It is rare in everyday conversation today and is mostly heard in manga and anime.
「ですぞ」 and 「ますぞ」 sound like an old man or a stock character and are not used in normal modern speech.

daily.title: Hurrying the family in the morning
daily.description: A father tells his kid to hurry up and get out the door.
daily.example: It's already eight o'clock. Get up!

daily.title: Inviting friends out
daily.description: Guys making plans to hang out.
daily.example: Let's go to the beach this weekend.

daily.title: Watching manga or anime
daily.description: A hot-blooded hero psyches himself up before a fight.
daily.example: I am absolutely not going to lose!

work.title: Sports practice
work.description: A coach or captain shouts to the team. Typical of sports or on-site work.
work.example: Five more minutes! Run to the end!

etymology: 「ぞ」 comes from the classical emphatic particle 「ぞ」 (as in the 「〜ぞ〜ける」 construction), which later moved to the end of the sentence for emphasis. 「ぜ」 is thought to be a contraction of forms like 「ぞえ」 in Edo-period speech. It was once used by everyone but later became masculine.

similar.title: 〜よ
similar.explanation: 「よ」 tells the listener something they don't know; it's gender-neutral and gentle. 「ぞ」 and 「ぜ」 are more forceful and strongly masculine.

similar.title: 〜さ (sentence-final particle)
similar.explanation: 「さ」 sounds casual and matter-of-fact (平気さ). 「ぞ」 and 「ぜ」 emphasize and assert strongly.

similar.title: 〜ね
similar.explanation: 「ね」 seeks the listener's agreement. 「ぞ」 and 「ぜ」 one-sidedly stress your own judgment or resolve.

meaning: Shows that something isn't limited to one person, region, or field, but reaches much further: “not just ... (but also ...)”. Written language.
connection: ひとり + noun + のみならず / だけでなく / にとどまらず

senses.label: Not merely ...
senses.meaning: First names one thing, then says the problem or effect reaches a wider scope. 「ひとり」 stresses “just this one”. Formal; used for social issues and commentary.
senses.connection: ひとり + noun + のみならず, 〜も / 〜全体 (ひとり日本のみならず, ひとり若者だけでなく)
examples: Environmental problems are not Japan's alone but a challenge for the whole world.
This recession is affecting not only small and medium businesses but large companies too.
The falling birthrate is serious not only in rural areas but in cities as well.

senses.label: Not just a problem of ...
senses.meaning: Forms like 「ひとり〜の問題ではない」 or 「ひとり〜にとどまらない」 reject the view that something concerns only one party and stress that it involves everyone.
senses.connection: ひとり + noun + の問題ではない / にとどまらない
examples: Bullying is not just a school problem but a problem for society as a whole.
Its impact goes beyond the industry itself.

notes: Here 「ひとり」 is an adverb meaning “merely, solely”. It has nothing to do with “one person” and is usually written in kana.
This is very stiff written language, found in editorials, speeches, and papers. In conversation, 「〜だけでなく」 is enough.
The second half often widens the scope with words like 「〜も」, 「社会全体」, or 「世界中」.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news commentator discusses a social issue.
daily.example: Rising prices are squeezing not only household budgets but businesses as well.

daily.title: Reading an editorial
daily.description: An editorial urges people to care about the aging population.
daily.example: An aging society is not a problem for the elderly alone.

work.title: Writing a report
work.description: A research report points out how widespread a problem is.
work.example: The labor shortage is not just our company's issue; it has become a challenge for the entire industry.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: A paper explains how common a phenomenon is.
work.example: This tendency is seen not only in Japanese but in many other languages.

etymology: 「ひとり」 is written 「独り」 and originally means “alone, single”. As an adverb it came to mean “merely, solely”, and is often followed by a negative or 「のみならず」. 「のみならず」 is the limiting particle 「のみ」 plus the classical negative 「ならず」 (“is not”), meaning “not only”.

similar.title: 〜のみならず
similar.explanation: 「〜のみならず」 alone means “not only”. Adding 「ひとり」 stresses “just this one thing”, making the widening of scope stronger and more literary.

similar.title: 〜ただ〜のみならず
similar.explanation: 「ただ〜のみならず」 means almost the same as 「ひとり〜のみならず」. 「ひとり」 usually takes nouns for people, organizations, or places, while 「ただ」 is used more broadly.

similar.title: 〜だけでなく
similar.explanation: 「〜だけでなく」 is the everyday expression, fine in speech or writing. 「ひとり〜のみならず」 is solemn written language.

meaning: Takes some event as a good moment to end something you've been doing or to start something new: “taking ... as an opportunity”.
connection: Noun + を潮に (して) / を潮として

senses.label: Taking the chance to stop
senses.meaning: Treats an event as “just the right moment” to end something ongoing, like ending a party, leaving, retiring, or quitting smoking. Usually for decisions you make yourself.
senses.connection: Noun + を潮に + 引退する / やめる / お開きにする (定年を潮に, これを潮に)
examples: With the president's speech as the cue, the party came to an end.
He retired from active work on his sixtieth birthday.
When my child was born, I took the chance to quit smoking.

senses.label: Taking the chance to start
senses.meaning: Can also mean using a moment to start something new or change direction, but there's still often a sense of saying goodbye to the past.
senses.connection: Noun + を潮に (して) + 始める / 転職する / 故郷に帰る
examples: I took my marriage as the moment to move back to my hometown.
I'm going to use this as a chance to make a fresh start.

notes: 「潮」 originally means the timing of the tides. Here it means “the right moment”, and the second half is usually an action of ending or leaving.
This is fairly formal and a little literary. In conversation, 「〜をきっかけに」 is more common.
The set phrases 「これを潮に」 and 「それを潮に」 are common, meaning “and with that, ...”.

daily.title: Ending a party
daily.description: When a party has gone on for a while, someone takes the chance to suggest wrapping up.
daily.example: It's started raining, so let's call it a night.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character in a novel uses something as a chance to leave.
daily.example: When the phone rang, he took the chance to get up from his seat.

work.title: Retirement speech
work.description: At a farewell party, someone explains why they're retiring.
work.example: With my reaching retirement age, I have decided to step down from the front line.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on a company pulling out of a business.
work.example: Following this loss, the company withdrew from its overseas business.

etymology: 「潮」 means the tide. 「潮時 (しおどき)」 was the moment of high or low tide, when fishermen and boatmen had to judge when to set out or come back. It came to mean “the right time to do something”. 「〜を潮に」 means “treating ... as that moment”, so it's often used for stopping or ending.

similar.title: 〜をきっかけに
similar.explanation: 「〜をきっかけに」 is the general “triggered by ...” and works for things that start by chance. 「〜を潮に」 stresses seizing the moment to wrap something up, so it's mostly for ending or withdrawing.

similar.title: 〜を契機に
similar.explanation: 「〜を契機に」 is written language for major turning points or social change. 「〜を潮に」 is mostly for personal decisions to leave, retire, or end a gathering.

similar.title: 〜を限りに
similar.explanation: 「〜を限りに」 marks a point in time as the cutoff (今日を限りに). 「〜を潮に」 treats an event as the right moment.

similar.title: 〜を境に
similar.explanation: 「〜を境に」 objectively shows that things changed before and after a point. 「〜を潮に」 shows actively seizing a moment to act.

meaning: Follows a number to mean “no less than, at least”, stressing how large the amount is. Written language.
connection: Number + を下らない (を下らず)

senses.label: No less than
senses.meaning: The real amount is at least the stated number, and probably more. The speaker wants to stress that it's large. Common in estimates in news and reports.
senses.connection: Number + を下らない (〜人を下らない, 〜億円を下らない)
examples: Damage from this earthquake is estimated at no less than one trillion yen.
No fewer than ten thousand people attended the rally.
This painting is probably worth no less than 500 million yen.

senses.label: Formal linking forms
senses.meaning: 「〜を下らず」 links clauses mid-sentence, and 「〜を下らぬ」 modifies a noun. Same meaning, more formal.
senses.connection: Number + を下らず, ... / を下らぬ + noun
examples: The death toll is no less than a thousand, and the damage is still spreading.
Every year, no fewer than a hundred inquiries come in.

notes: Only used with fairly large numbers to stress “a lot”. Small numbers like 「三人を下らない」 are not used.
Don't confuse it with the adjective 「くだらない」 (“trivial, worthless”). 「くだらない話」 means “a silly story”.
Here 「下る」 means “to fall below (a value)”, written with the kanji 「下」.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news report on the scale of a disaster or accident.
daily.example: Reportedly, no fewer than a hundred houses burned down in this fire.

daily.title: Talking about a collector
daily.description: Friends talk about someone's art collection.
daily.example: Apparently that guy owns no fewer than a thousand paintings.

work.title: Market research report
work.description: A report estimates the size of a market.
work.example: The number of potential customers in Japan is estimated at no fewer than five million.

work.title: Business news
work.description: A report on a company's losses.
work.example: The cost of this recall is expected to be no less than ten billion yen.

etymology: 「下る (くだる)」 originally means “to go down”, and by extension “(a value) to fall below”. 「〜を下らない」 literally means “doesn't fall below ...”, hence “at least ...”. The adjective 「くだらない」 (“trivial”) comes from the same root, but the meanings have split apart.

similar.title: 〜からある／〜からする
similar.explanation: 「〜からある」 also stresses a large amount, mostly for concrete things like weight, length, or price (十キロからある荷物). 「〜を下らない」 is mostly used with statistics and estimates.

similar.title: 〜にのぼる
similar.explanation: 「〜にのぼる」 means an amount actually “reaches” a large number, a confirmed result. 「〜を下らない」 means “at least” and is usually an estimate.

similar.title: 〜以上
similar.explanation: 「〜以上」 is the neutral “or more”. 「〜を下らない」 is more formal and carries surprise at how large the amount is.

meaning: Shows that the result is in proportion to what came before: “you get back as much as you put in”. Both sides rise or fall together.

senses.label: You get what you put in
senses.meaning: The effort in the first half and the reward in the second are proportional: “the more you ..., the more ...”. Often about effort or practice and results, with an encouraging tone.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + 分だけ + 結果が出る / うまくなる / 報われる
examples: The effort you put in will always pay off accordingly.
The more you practice, the better you get.
The harder it was, the greater the joy.

senses.label: Making up for it
senses.meaning: Shows that a gap caused by the first half must be made up by the same amount in the second: “as much as you ..., you have to ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + 分 (だけ), 〜なければならない / 取り戻す
examples: I took time off, so tomorrow I have to work that much harder.
I worked overtime to make up for the delay.

notes: 「分」 is read 「ぶん」 here, meaning “share, corresponding amount”. Don't read it as 「ふん」 (minutes).
It can also follow adjectives, as in 「高い分だけ品質もいい」 (it's pricier, but the quality is better to match). Still, the verb ta-form is most common.
The 「だけ」 in 「分だけ」 can be dropped: 「努力した分、報われる」.

daily.title: Encouraging a friend before an exam
daily.description: Your friend is nervous before an exam, so you cheer them up.
daily.example: Everything you studied will count, so you'll be fine.

daily.title: After a workout
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about dieting.
daily.example: If you don't move as much as you eat, you'll gain weight fast.

daily.title: Splitting costs after a trip
daily.description: Friends dividing up expenses.
daily.example: Just pay for what you used.

work.title: A boss encouraging the team
work.description: A manager motivates the team at the start of a project.
work.example: The more time we spend preparing, the more relaxed we'll be on the day.

work.title: Explaining pricing
work.description: Explaining pay-as-you-go pricing to a customer.
work.example: Please pay only for what you actually use.

etymology: 「分 (ぶん)」 originally means “a divided portion, one's share”, and by extension “a corresponding degree”. 「〜た分だけ」 means “as much as the portion you did”, expressing a proportional relationship.

similar.title: 〜ば〜ほど
similar.explanation: 「〜ば〜ほど」 means “the more ..., the more ...”, focusing on a trend of change. 「〜た分だけ」 focuses on effort and result matching one-to-one.

similar.title: 〜だけ (extent)
similar.explanation: 「〜だけ」 means “as much as possible, within the limits of” (できるだけ). 「〜た分だけ」 means getting results in proportion to what you did.

similar.title: 〜にしたがって
similar.explanation: 「〜にしたがって」 shows one thing changing along with another, often a natural trend. 「〜た分だけ」 is mostly about personal effort and reward.

meaning: Adds an explanation of the reason for what was just said: “The reason is that ...”.
connection: (Previous sentence.) というのも + plain form + からだ

senses.label: Adding a reason
senses.meaning: First state a result or situation, then bring in the cause with 「というのも」. The sentence often ends with 「からだ」 or 「のだ」. Softer than 「なぜなら」; common in narratives and explanations.
senses.connection: 〜。というのも、plain form + からだ / のだ (nouns / na-adjectives: 〜だからだ)
examples: I haven't been sleeping well lately. That's because the construction next door is so noisy.
He's off today. The reason is that he's had a fever since yesterday.
This shop is always crowded. That's because it's cheap.

senses.label: それというのも
senses.meaning: Adding 「それ」 gives 「それというのも」, which points back to the previous sentence more clearly and sounds more formal. Common in writing.
senses.connection: 〜。それというのも、plain form + からだ / のである
examples: The plan ended in failure. This was because preparation was insufficient.
It's no wonder he succeeded. After all, he worked harder than anyone.

notes: 「というのも」 usually starts a sentence and follows on from the previous one. It can't open a conversation on its own.
「からだ」 is the most common ending, but 「のだ」 or 「ためだ」 also work. In speech it can be omitted.
In 「彼が怒ったというのも無理はない」, 「というのも」 means “the fact that ... too”. That's not this pattern.

daily.title: Explaining why you're late
daily.description: Telling a friend why you arrived late.
daily.example: Sorry I'm late. The train stopped, you see.

daily.title: Writing a blog or diary
daily.description: Explaining a recent change in your diary.
daily.example: I've started cooking lately. That's because I got tired of eating out.

work.title: Explaining to your boss
work.description: Reporting that a deadline will slip and why.
work.example: The delivery is likely to be delayed. This is because parts are arriving late.

work.title: Writing an analysis report
work.description: A report analyzes why sales grew.
work.example: Sales exceeded last year's. This is because the new product was well received.

etymology: Made of the quoting 「と」 + 「いう」 + the nominalizer 「の」 + the particle 「も」. Literally “speaking of (this) ...”, it introduces an explanation of the previous statement and pairs with 「からだ」 at the end.

similar.title: なぜなら〜からだ
similar.explanation: 「なぜなら」 is logical and stiff, like making an argument. 「というのも」 is softer and more narrative, often used when telling a story or explaining background.

similar.title: 〜のは〜からだ
similar.explanation: 「〜のは〜からだ」 links result and reason in one sentence. 「というのも〜からだ」 starts a new sentence after the first to add the reason.

similar.title: 〜というのは
similar.explanation: 「〜というのは」 is mostly for definitions or explaining a word (〜というのは〜のことだ). 「というのも」 is only for adding a reason.

meaning: Whenever the first thing happens, the second always follows: “every time ..., without fail”. Describes habits or regular patterns.
connection: Verb dictionary form + と決まって + ...

senses.label: Without fail
senses.meaning: As soon as the first thing happens, the second happens every single time. Often for someone's habits or quirks, or recurring phenomena. The second half is usually present tense or 「〜たものだ」.
senses.connection: Dictionary form + と決まって + verb (酒を飲むと決まって, 雨が降ると決まって)
examples: Whenever my father drinks, he always starts talking about the old days.
Every time it rains, I get a headache without fail.
Right before an exam, I always get an upset stomach.

senses.label: Always when ...
senses.meaning: The adverb 「決まって」 can also go with 「〜時は」, 「〜たびに」, etc., meaning “whenever ..., always ...”.
senses.connection: 〜時は / 〜たびに / 〜日は + 決まって + verb
examples: On Sundays, our family always goes for a walk together.
Whenever she's in trouble, she always calls her mother.

notes: The second half must be something that happens repeatedly, not a one-time event.
「〜と決まっている」 (it's been decided) and 「〜に決まっている」 (it must be) are different. Check whether 「いる」 follows 「決まって」.
For past habits, use 「〜と決まって〜たものだ」.

daily.title: Talking about family habits
daily.description: Telling a friend about your grandfather.
daily.example: Whenever his grandkids visit, my grandpa always gives them pocket money.

daily.title: Grumbling about your health
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about catching colds when seasons change.
daily.example: I always catch a cold when the seasons change.

daily.title: Childhood memories
daily.description: Telling a friend a story from when you were little.
daily.example: As a kid, I always went to my grandma's house every summer vacation.

work.title: Chatting with coworkers
work.description: Complaining about a machine's old problem.
work.example: This copier always jams right when you're in a hurry.

work.title: Writing an analysis report
work.description: Describing a market pattern.
work.example: Whenever the economy slows down, sales of cheap products always go up.

etymology: 「決まる」 means “to be decided, fixed”. Its te-form 「決まって」 works as an adverb meaning “invariably, as usual”. With the conditional 「と」 before it, it gives “whenever ..., invariably ...”.

similar.title: 〜たびに
similar.explanation: 「〜たびに」 means “each time ...”, focusing on every occurrence. 「〜と決まって」 focuses on “always, without exception”. They are often interchangeable.

similar.title: 〜と (conditional)
similar.explanation: 「〜と」 alone can also express a habitual condition. Adding 「決まって」 stresses that it happens every time without fail.

similar.title: 〜に決まっている
similar.explanation: 「〜に決まっている」 is the speaker's confident judgment: “it must be ...”. 「〜と決まって」 describes a recurring pattern.

meaning: Shows that something looks one way on the surface but is actually not: “it seems ..., but actually ...”.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form, na-adjective + な, noun + の + ようでいて

senses.label: Seems ... but actually
senses.meaning: The first half is the impression something gives; the second points out the opposite reality. Often paired with 「実は」, 「意外と」, or 「案外」. Has a reflective “when you think about it, it isn't so” feel.
senses.connection: Plain form + ようでいて, 実は / 意外と〜 (簡単なようでいて, 知っているようでいて)
examples: This problem looks easy, but it's actually quite hard.
We think we know ourselves, but we often don't.
He seems laid-back, but he works really fast.

senses.label: Both ... and ...
senses.meaning: Shows that one thing has two seemingly contradictory sides: “it's ..., and yet also ...”. Often used to describe personalities, works of art, or scenery; a literary tone.
senses.connection: Noun + の / na-adjective + な + ようでいて, 〜でもある
examples: That song sounds cheerful, yet somehow it leaves you feeling lonely.
His manner seems cold, but there's kindness in it too.

notes: Stronger than 「〜ようで」; it emphasizes the gap between appearance and reality.
Mostly used in writing and fairly formal conversation. Very common in essays and reviews.
In 「元気なようで安心した」 (“I'm relieved you seem well”), 「ようで」 is inference plus reason, not this pattern.

daily.title: Describing a friend
daily.description: Talking about a friend who seems careless.
daily.example: She seems sloppy, but she notices the little details.

daily.title: Sharing study tips
daily.description: Japanese learners trade thoughts on studying.
daily.example: Keigo looks simple, but it's hard to master.

work.title: Book or film review
work.description: A review analyzes what makes a work special.
work.example: This novel seems like a simple love story, but it contains sharp social criticism.

work.title: Discussing an issue in a meeting
work.description: Explaining that a task is not as easy as it looks.
work.example: This task looks simple, but it actually takes experience.

etymology: Formed from 「ようで」, the continuative form of 「ようだ」 (appearance, comparison), plus 「いて」, the te-form of 「いる」. It means “being in a state of seeming ...”. When followed by a contrast, it gives “it seems ..., but actually ...”.

similar.title: 〜ようだ・〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: 「〜ようだ」 is just a guess or comparison. 「〜ようでいて」 always involves a contrast, pointing out that reality differs from appearances.

similar.title: 〜ながら（も） (concessive)
similar.explanation: 「〜ながらも」 means “although it's true that ..., ...”; the first half is a fact. In 「〜ようでいて」, the first half is only an outward impression.

similar.title: 〜かのようだ
similar.explanation: 「〜かのようだ」 means “as if ...”, usually an unreal comparison. 「〜ようでいて」 stresses “it seems so, but actually isn't”.

meaning: Shows that an amount reaches a large number: “amounts to, totals as many as”. Can also mean that something comes up as a topic.

senses.label: Amounts to
senses.meaning: An amount or sum reaches a fairly large number, with a feeling of “that many!”. Common for statistics in news and reports.
senses.connection: Number + にのぼる / にのぼった (〜人にのぼる, 〜億円に上る)
examples: The number of dead and injured in this accident reached one hundred.
Total damage is expected to amount to five billion yen.
Sales of this product reach three million units a year.

senses.label: Coming up as a topic
senses.meaning: Used with nouns like 「話題」, 「議題」, or 「口」 to mean “to be brought up, to be put up for discussion”.
senses.connection: 話題 / 議題 / 口の端 / 食卓 + に上る
examples: That matter was put on the meeting's agenda.
His name has been coming up a lot lately.

notes: Used with fairly large numbers to stress “a lot”. Small numbers (三人にのぼる) sound unnatural.
For amounts it is usually written 「にのぼる」, also 「に上る」. Distinguish it from the physical action in 「階段を上る」 (climb the stairs).
The past 「〜にのぼった」 is often used in reports of figures already counted.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news report gives disaster statistics.
daily.example: Reportedly, as many as ten thousand residents were evacuated.

daily.title: Talking about a hot topic
daily.description: A friend mentions something everyone's talking about.
daily.example: That drama comes up a lot at my office too.

work.title: Annual report
work.description: A report describes growth in users.
work.example: Membership reached two million as of the end of last fiscal year.

work.title: Meeting minutes
work.description: Recording that an issue was raised for discussion.
work.example: The issue of cost cutting was put on the agenda again.

etymology: 「のぼる」 is written 「上る／昇る」 and originally means “to go up, rise”. From physical rising it extended to an amount “rising to (a value)” and to being “raised (as a topic or agenda item)”.

similar.title: 〜を下らない
similar.explanation: 「〜を下らない」 means “at least ...”, usually an estimate. 「〜にのぼる」 means an amount actually “reaches” a large number.

similar.title: 〜に至る
similar.explanation: 「〜に至る」 means a situation “reaches” a stage or place, not specifically a number. 「〜にのぼる」 is only for amounts or topics.

similar.title: 〜に達する
similar.explanation: 「〜に達する」 objectively states reaching a standard or value, and works with smaller numbers too. 「〜にのぼる」 carries amazement at how large the amount is.

meaning: Shows going along with someone else's wishes or your own mood without resisting: “just as ... told me, at the mercy of, following wherever ... leads”.
connection: Verb passive form / dictionary form + ままに; noun + の + 赴くままに

senses.label: Doing what others say
senses.meaning: With the passive form, it means you have no will of your own and simply do what others say or suggest. Often implies passivity, regret, or resignation.
senses.connection: Verb passive form + ままに (言われるままに, 勧められるままに, 誘われるままに)
examples: I let the salesclerk talk me into buying expensive clothes.
I signed the documents just as I was told.
My friend invited me, so I just went along to the party.

senses.label: Following your heart
senses.meaning: With words for feelings or desires like 「思う」, 「向く」, or 「赴く」, it means acting as your heart or whim leads: “wherever the mood takes you”.
senses.connection: 思う / 感じる + ままに; 気の向く / 足の向く / 心の赴く + ままに
examples: I set off on a trip alone, wherever the mood took me.
I write in my diary whatever comes to mind.
I want to live as my heart leads me.

senses.label: At someone's mercy
senses.meaning: 「〜されるがまま」 and 「なすがまま」 mean not resisting at all and letting others do as they please.
senses.connection: Verb passive form + がまま (に); なすがまま
examples: He just let them do whatever they wanted to him.
Carried along by the waves, the boat drifted out to sea.

notes: 「〜まま」 originally means “as it is”. Here it extends to “just as ..., following ...”.
The 「に」 in 「ままに」 is sometimes dropped: 「言われるまま、契約した」.
「わがまま」 (selfish) is a separate word and not related to this pattern.

daily.title: Regretting an impulse buy
daily.description: Complaining to a friend that a salesperson talked you into it.
daily.example: The salesman talked me into signing a contract.

daily.title: A weekend walk
daily.description: Telling a friend you wandered around all day without a plan.
daily.example: I just wandered around an unfamiliar town, going wherever my feet took me.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character's helplessness.
daily.example: The girl had lived her life drifting wherever fate carried her.

work.title: Reflecting on how you work
work.description: At a training session, someone says you can't just follow orders.
work.example: If you only do what your boss tells you, you won't grow.

work.title: News about a scam
work.description: A report about a victim tricked into a transfer.
work.example: The victim transferred cash exactly as the caller instructed.

etymology: 「まま」 is written 「儘」 and originally means “as it is, just as ...”. With the passive or verbs of feeling, it becomes “acting just as (someone's will) directs”, and from there “at the mercy of”.

similar.title: 〜ままに (following)
similar.explanation: The meaning is the same. This entry focuses on the passive 「〜られるままに」 and set phrases like 「気の向くままに」.

similar.title: 〜まま
similar.explanation: 「〜たまま」 means a state stays unchanged (靴を履いたまま). 「〜られるままに」 means going along with others or your feelings.

similar.title: 〜にしたがって
similar.explanation: 「〜にしたがって」 means actively following rules or instructions, in a neutral tone. 「〜られるままに」 implies having no will of your own and not resisting.

meaning: Shows that everything is ready and only the last step remains: “all that's left is to ..., ready to go”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + ばかりになっている

senses.label: Just waiting to ...
senses.meaning: All the other preparations are done, and only the final action is left: “all that's left is to ..., ready to ... any time”. Often with 「あとは」 or 「もう」.
senses.connection: Dictionary form + ばかりになっている / ばかりになっていた (食べるばかり, 出発するばかり)
examples: The food is ready; it just needs to be put on the table.
The packing is done, and all that's left is to leave.
All the documents were ready; they just had to be submitted.

senses.label: Got everything ready
senses.meaning: 「〜ばかりにしてある／しておく」 means deliberately getting things ready so only the last step is left.
senses.connection: Dictionary form + ばかりにしてある / ばかりにしておく
examples: I've got everything ready so all I have to do is change, so I can head out anytime.
I got the pot ready so it only needs to go on the stove.

notes: Only follows the dictionary form, showing a final step that hasn't happened yet.
「あとは〜ばかりだ」 is similar and very common, as in 「あとは結果を待つばかりだ」.
Don't confuse it with 「〜ばかりだ」 (keeps getting ..., only ...) or 「〜たばかり」 (just did).

daily.title: Getting ready to move
daily.description: Telling a friend the moving prep is all done.
daily.example: Everything's packed in boxes; all that's left is to carry it out.

daily.title: Dinner at home
daily.description: Everything is ready before the family gets home.
daily.example: Dinner just needs to be heated up, so go ahead and eat.

work.title: Before a system launch
work.description: Reporting to your boss on preparations.
work.example: The new system is all set and ready to go live.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on a new facility about to open.
work.example: The new station building is finished and just waiting to open.

etymology: 「ばかり」 was originally an adverbial particle of “degree, approximate extent” (from the verb 「はかる」, to measure). It came to mean “only, nothing but”. 「〜するばかりになっている」 means “being in a state where only ... remains”, so everything else is done.

similar.title: 〜ばかりだ (keeps getting ...)
similar.explanation: 「〜ばかりだ」 means a situation keeps getting worse (悪くなるばかりだ). 「〜ばかりになっている」 means everything is ready except the last step.

similar.title: 〜たばかり
similar.explanation: 「〜たばかり」 follows the ta-form and means “just did”. 「〜ばかりになっている」 follows the dictionary form and means “just waiting to do”.

similar.title: 〜んばかりに
similar.explanation: 「〜んばかりに」 means “as if about to ...”, a figure of speech. 「〜ばかりになっている」 describes an actual state of readiness.

meaning: Expresses heartfelt relief or happiness about a situation: “I'm so glad that ..., nothing could be better”.
connection: Verb te-form / i-adjective くて / noun, na-adjective + で + 何よりだ

senses.label: Happy for someone
senses.meaning: Expresses relief that the other person is safe, healthy, or doing well. A common phrase in greetings and letters; sincere and polite.
senses.connection: お元気そうで / ご無事で / お変わりなくて + 何よりです
examples: I'm so glad to see you looking well.
I'm delighted that everyone is doing well.
I'm so glad you liked it.

senses.label: Glad about the outcome
senses.meaning: Relief about how things turned out: “(whatever else happened,) this is what matters most”. Often used for a silver lining.
senses.connection: 無事で / けががなくて / 間に合って + 何よりだ
examples: I was in an accident, but thank goodness I wasn't hurt.
We lost the game, but the main thing is everyone's safe.

notes: Mostly used about other people or the overall situation. For your own good news, 「よかった」 sounds more natural.
The polite 「〜て何よりです」 is very common in opening greetings of letters and emails.
In 「何よりも大切だ」 (more important than anything), 「何より」 is an adverb, not this pattern.

daily.title: Seeing someone after a long time
daily.description: Greeting an older relative you haven't seen in ages.
daily.example: Grandma, I'm so glad to see you looking so well.

daily.title: A friend leaves the hospital
daily.description: Calling a friend after they're discharged.
daily.example: I'm so glad you got out of the hospital safely.

work.title: Opening a business email
work.description: A greeting in an email to a client.
work.example: I trust everyone is keeping well, and I am very glad to hear it.

work.title: At the end of a project
work.description: A manager expresses relief that the team finished smoothly.
work.example: I'm glad it all wrapped up without any major problems.

etymology: 「何より」 means “more than anything”, made of the question word 「何」 plus 「より」 of comparison. With a te-form of cause before it, it means “because ..., it's better than anything”, i.e., “I'm so glad that ...”.

similar.title: 〜てよかった
similar.explanation: 「〜てよかった」 is the everyday “I'm glad that ...” and works for your own news. 「〜て何よりだ」 is more formal and mostly used for relief about others or the overall situation.

similar.title: 〜に越したことはない
similar.explanation: 「〜に越したことはない」 means “it's best to ...”, a general piece of advice. 「〜て何よりだ」 expresses relief at a good result that has already happened.
